interviewQuestions.question: Design the serving path for a real-time fraud-scoring model.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd start by naming the hard constraint: a fraud decision has to happen within the transaction flow, typically under 100ms, so this is unambiguously an online-serving problem, not batch. I'd containerize the model behind a low-latency serving layer (gRPC internally for speed, since this is a service-to-service call, not a public API), load the model into memory once at startup, and put it behind a load balancer with multiple replicas for both throughput and redundancy — a fraud endpoint going down can't simply queue requests for later. For features, I'd pull precomputed features from a low-latency online feature store rather than computing them on the fly, to keep the request path fast and to guarantee the exact same feature values the model saw in training (avoiding training-serving skew). Before ever serving live traffic, I'd run the new model in shadow deployment against the current production model to compare behavior with zero user risk, then roll out via a canary (a small traffic percentage) while monitoring both model-level metrics (score distributions) and business metrics (fraud caught, false-positive rate on legitimate transactions), ramping up only if those stay healthy, with an instant rollback path if not. I'd close by noting monitoring doesn't stop at launch — fraud patterns drift, so this needs ongoing drift detection and a retraining trigger, not a one-time deployment.

**Testing:** whether you can design an end-to-end serving path — latency budget, feature consistency, safe rollout, ongoing monitoring — rather than just naming "deploy it behind an API".
interviewQuestions.subTitle: End-to-end low-latency serving design

interviewQuestions.question: What's the actual difference between shadow deployment and a canary release, and why would you use both rather than picking one?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
They answer genuinely different questions and carry genuinely different risk profiles, which is why mature rollouts use both in sequence rather than treating them as interchangeable safe-rollout options. Shadow deployment runs the new model alongside the current production model on real live traffic, but its predictions are logged only and never returned to any user — this means it carries zero user-facing risk no matter how badly the new model behaves, since nothing it outputs ever reaches a real decision. Its purpose is narrowly: does this model behave reasonably on real, current traffic patterns, compared side by side against the model it would replace? It catches gross problems (wildly different prediction distributions, crashes on real inputs, obvious bugs) cheaply and safely before the new model has ever influenced anything real.

A canary release goes further and accepts real, contained risk: a small slice of real traffic (often 5%) has its predictions actually used, while the rest continues on the old model. This answers a different, harder question that shadow deployment structurally cannot: does the new model actually perform well when its predictions have real consequences for real users? Shadow deployment can miss subtle issues that only show up when predictions actually drive downstream behavior — for instance, if the new model interacts with a feedback loop (its predictions influence what data gets collected next), shadow mode never exercises that loop since its outputs are discarded.

Using both in sequence — shadow first to catch gross issues at zero risk, then canary to validate real performance at contained risk, then full rollout — is strictly safer than skipping straight to canary, since it filters out entire categories of bug before any real user is exposed to them.

**Testing:** whether you can articulate the specific risk/question trade-off each stage answers, not just that both exist as generic rollout best practices.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Shadow deployment vs canary release, and why use both

interviewQuestions.question: Your team defaults to always building a real-time online-serving endpoint for every new model, even ones that feed weekly reports. What's the cost of that default, and when is it actually justified?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The cost is real and easy to underestimate because it's ongoing infrastructure spend rather than a one-time engineering cost: an always-on serving endpoint means paying for standby compute capacity even when idle, maintaining a load balancer and health checks, handling scaling and failover for a service that in this case never actually needs to respond in milliseconds, and carrying the operational burden of an always-running service (alerting, on-call, security patching) for a workload whose actual requirement was "give me a number sometime before next week's report." None of that infrastructure cost buys anything for a use case that could tolerate hours of latency — it's pure overhead relative to the actual requirement.

Online serving is justified specifically when a prediction is needed the instant a request happens and there's no tolerance for delay — fraud scoring at checkout, live search ranking, a chat response — situations where the caller is actively waiting and a batch-computed stale answer would be actively wrong or useless. For anything that can be precomputed on a schedule and read from storage later — a weekly churn-risk score, a nightly recommendation refresh — batch scoring gets the same predictions at a fraction of the infrastructure cost, since it only pays for compute during the scheduled run rather than standby capacity around the clock.

My advice to a team defaulting to online serving "just in case" would be to make the online/batch decision explicit and match it to the actual latency requirement stated by the consuming use case, rather than defaulting to the more "impressive-sounding" real-time architecture regardless of whether anything actually needs it.

**Testing:** whether you can quantify the concrete cost of defaulting to online serving unnecessarily, not just state that batch is "cheaper" as an abstract fact.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: The cost of defaulting to online serving unnecessarily
